How to Become an AI Engineer in 6 Months (Without Wasting Time)

Forget trying to learn everything.

The goal isn't to memorize AI buzzwords. The goal is to become someone who can build real AI products.

By the end of six months, you should be able to:

• Build LLM applications from scratch
• Work with OpenAI, Anthropic, and open-source models
• Design effective prompts and AI workflows
• Integrate tools, memory, and structured outputs
• Deploy production-ready AI applications

Here's a roadmap I'd recommend.

Month 1: Programming & Backend Foundations

Before touching advanced AI, become comfortable with the tools you'll use every day.

Learn:

• Python
• Git & GitHub
• Terminal / CLI
• HTTP, REST APIs & JSON
• Async programming basics
• SQL
• Pandas
• Virtual environments
• Error handling
• FastAPI (or Flask)

Build:

• A REST API
• A small automation tool
• A CRUD application

Month 2: LLM Application Development

Now start building with language models.

Learn:

• Prompt engineering
• System vs User messages
• Structured outputs (JSON)
• Function / Tool Calling
• Streaming responses
• Conversation memory
• Token usage & cost optimization
• Failure handling
• Prompt injection prevention

Projects:

• AI Chatbot
• Text Summarizer
• AI Writing Assistant

Month 3: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Most useful AI products rely on retrieval.

Learn:

• Embeddings
• Chunking strategies
• Vector databases
• Metadata filtering
• Hybrid search
• Reranking
• Hallucination reduction
• Grounded responses & citations

Projects:

• Chat with PDFs
• Documentation Assistant
• Internal Knowledge Base Chatbot

Month 4: AI Agents & Workflows

Agents are powerful, but only when used correctly.

Learn:

• Agent loops
• Tool selection
• State management
• Multi-step workflows
• Retry mechanisms
• Evaluation pipelines
• Success metrics
• When NOT to use agents

Projects:

• Research Agent
• Coding Assistant
• Multi-tool Workflow Automation

Month 5: Production & Deployment

Building locally isn't enough.

Learn:

• Production FastAPI
• Docker
• Background jobs
• Queues
• Authentication
• API security
• Logging
• Monitoring & observability
• Prompt versioning
• Cost monitoring
• Rate limiting
• Caching

Projects:

• Deploy an AI SaaS
• Add monitoring dashboards
• Support multiple users

Month 6: Choose Your Path

Don't try to master every area.

Pick one direction and go deep.

Direction 1: AI Product Engineer

Best for startup jobs.

Focus on:

• LLM applications
• RAG
• AI Agents
• Deployment
• Product UX

Direction 2: Applied AI / LLM Engineer

Focus on:

• Fine-tuning
• Prompting vs Fine-tuning
• Model evaluation
• Inference optimization
• Open-source models
• Training pipelines

Direction 3: AI Automation Engineer

Focus on:

• Workflow orchestration
• Multi-tool systems
• CRM automation
• Email & document automation
• Business process automation

This roadmap is only valuable if you actually build while learning.

Every concept should turn into a project.

By the end of six months, you'll have a portfolio full of real AI applications instead of just certificates.

Save this roadmap. You'll thank yourself later.

STOP SCREENSHOTTING KIMI K3 BENCHMARKS. ROUTE REAL WORK TO IT

Moonshot shipped Kimi K3 on July 16 with 2.8 trillion parameters, 1M context, native text/image/video input and $3 per million input tokens

Most people will treat it like launch-week content

Post the benchmark chart, argue in replies, then send zero real tasks through the model

That misses the actual use case

K3 is not trying to be the smartest model in every situation

It is a volume machine

The important part is the 1M context window, flat long-context pricing, and cache hits at $0.30 per million tokens

That changes the economics of heavy work

Repo-wide analysis. Large docs. Research corpora. Agent loops that reread the same context again and again

A normal setup pays full price every time the model sees the same project

A structured setup keeps the stable context identical, puts the new task last, and lets cache pricing cut repeated context by 10x

But the catch matters

Benchmarks are still self-reported. Reasoning effort is max-only at launch. Open weights are promised for July 27, not live yet. And trivial tasks can get expensive because the model overthinks them at full output price

So the move is not “replace your whole stack overnight”

The move is routing

Keep premium models on hard reasoning and sensitive work

Send long-context reading, repo analysis, doc synthesis and repeated agent context to K3

Most people are still asking which model is king

The winners are asking which task each model should own

Building an AI-powered builder tool has made me realize how difficult a truly general-purpose version would be.

The visible building is only one layer. Every floor, wall, staircase, and object also needs colliders. These are invisible meshes that stop people from walking through walls or falling through the floor.

An AI could dynamically design an entire scene, but it would also need to generate and coordinate that invisible structure correctly. You can make the problem easier by introducing a rigid building structure, but the more rigid it becomes, the less meaningful the AI design layer becomes.

I hesitate to call anything impossible right now. Still, this may simply be too difficult for most of us with the tools currently available.

That does not mean I am giving up on it. I am still going to try.

What I find more interesting is the direction this is pushing me toward.

I am starting to see my own building as a small ecosystem that needs an entire app to operate it. The app controls the building, its spaces, media, permissions, rewards, events, content, and user interactions.

That may be where app building inside virtual worlds becomes most useful.
